This isn’t innovation anymore — it’s a slow‑motion collapse disguised as genius.
The common thread across Tesla, SpaceX, xAI, and every Musk‑run company is simple: they are burning more money than they make, overpromising what they can’t deliver, and hiding operational chaos behind PR stunts. Tesla alone is projected to spend far more than it earns this year — a complete reversal from the “hyper‑profitable” narrative. SpaceX is drowning in costs, xAI is a money pit with no revenue model, and Twitter/X is losing cash at a rate that would get any other CEO fired instantly.

And the promises? They’re a decade old and still undelivered.
Full Self‑Driving was promised in 2016. It’s 2026. It still doesn’t exist.  
Not in the way it was sold. Not even close. People paid thousands for a feature that never arrived, and instead got a beta system that has triggered investigations, lawsuits, and fatal crashes. Families are suing because loved ones died. Employees are suing because of unsafe working conditions, discrimination, and retaliation. The list grows every month.

Meanwhile, Tesla’s product quality is going backwards.
Cars that used to have 14 speakers now have 7.
Cars that used to have ultrasonic sensors now have none.
Cars that used to have basic interior components now ship stripped down.
And somehow the price goes up, not down.
That’s not innovation — that’s desperation.

Battery degradation is another dirty secret.
Three years in and many owners are already down to 85% of their original range, and it only gets worse from there. Combine that with the reality of charging — 40 minutes on a “fast” charger if you’re lucky — and the ownership experience becomes a chore, not a breakthrough. The resale value collapse after every surprise price cut only adds insult to injury.

And the management?
It’s chaos.
No stable strategy. No accountability. No discipline.
One week Tesla is a car company.
The next week it’s an AI company.
Then a robotics company.
Then a robotaxi company.
Then a humanoid robot company.
Then a data company.
Then a subscription company.
It’s a roulette wheel, not a roadmap.

If any other CEO behaved like this — missing deadlines by years, torching cash, gutting product quality, facing waves of lawsuits, and making impulsive decisions that wipe out billions in shareholder value — they’d be removed immediately. Boards would intervene. Investors would revolt. Employees would walk.

But here, somehow, the chaos is treated like genius.

The truth is simple:
Everything is not okay. Everything is not stable. Everything is not sustainable.  
The cracks are showing across every company, every product line, every financial statement, and every broken promise. At some point, the hype runs out — and reality takes over. TESLA IS USELESS
